# Bond Fund Basics

## Overview

I keep a bond fund alongside the equity side of the portfolio, and I read its two headline figures before anything else. The first is duration, which on my fund sits at about 4.5 years. Duration is the sensitivity of the price to a change in interest rates: a duration of 4.5 means that a one percentage point rise in yields knocks roughly 4.5% off the price. The second figure is the yield to maturity, 4.1%, which is the return I would collect if I held every bond to the end and rates did nothing at all. The fund splits about 70% government and 30% corporate, so most of the credit risk sits in the smaller part. Government bonds carry the risk that a state delays or restructures its debt rather than the risk of a company failing, and the corporate slice adds a spread for the chance of default.

When rates rise, the price of the bonds in the fund falls, and the fund's net asset value falls with them, because the fund marks its holdings to the market each day. The fall is not a loss unless I sell, since a bond bought at a lower price still pays its coupon and still returns its face value at maturity. A rate rise is painful on paper and helpful on reinvestment, because the coupons coming in buy new bonds at the higher yield.

Credit risk is the other half of the story. A cut in a company's rating, or a default, lowers the value of those holdings and can widen the spread the market demands for the rest of the corporate slice. Short duration feels calmer because the price swings are smaller, which is why I keep the fund short rather than reaching for the longer end. Long bonds pay more when rates fall and hurt more when they rise, and I would rather not take that bet in the part of the portfolio meant to steady the rest.

## Notes

I check the fund's duration and yield to maturity every quarter, because both drift as the bonds inside mature and as the manager buys replacements. A fund that was short can become long without anyone announcing it. I read the split between government and corporate holdings at the same time, since a shift toward corporate credit lifts the yield and the risk in the same step. The 70/30 split I hold today is a deliberate middle ground: enough government paper to feel solid, enough corporate paper to pay a little more than a pure government fund.

I keep this money in a fund rather than in single bonds because a fund spreads a default across dozens of issuers instead of landing it on one. The trade is that I pay a management charge, small for a plain bond fund, and that the net asset value prints a price every day, which makes the swings visible where a single bond would sit quietly on the statement until maturity. I look at the running yield rather than only the yield to maturity when I care about the income, and I accept that the price will wander in the meantime. When the fund pays a distribution I put it back into the same fund, so the position keeps pace with the plan without a fresh decision every month. I also read the fund's published note on how it treats a temporary cash build-up, because a pile of idle money earns nothing and quietly drags the yield. A fund that holds its cash short and reinvests promptly tends to track its stated yield more closely than one that sits on the proceeds for a fortnight.

## Troubleshooting

The common confusion is a falling price after a rate rise. That is the fund working as designed, not breaking, and the coupon still arrives. I check that the drop roughly matches duration times the rate change before I look for anything stranger. A second case is a corporate holding whose rating is cut, which shows up as a small hit to the net asset value and a wider spread on the rest of the corporate slice; I watch the split and the largest holdings if it happens. The third is a fund that quietly extended its duration to chase yield, which I catch by comparing the current figure with the one in my note. If duration has risen well past what I chose, I either accept the new risk on purpose or shift the money to a shorter fund that matches the job I gave it. A duration I did not choose is a risk I did not ask for, and the published figure is the only honest source for it.
